faq.q: How does skin feel hot and cold?
faq.a: Skin has cold sensors and warm sensors, which are nerve endings with special temperature-sensitive channels. As skin cools, cold sensors fire more; as it warms, warm sensors fire more, and the brain compares them.

faq.q: Why does metal feel colder than wood?
faq.a: Metal conducts heat very well, so it draws warmth out of your skin quickly, and your cold sensors fire strongly. Wood conducts poorly, so your skin stays warmer, even though both are at the same temperature.
asks: Why does a metal bench feel cold?

faq.q: Why does lukewarm water feel hot after playing in snow?
faq.a: Temperature sensors adapt to the temperature they are used to. After cold snow, your hands judge lukewarm water against that cold starting point, so it feels hot.
asks: Why does water feel hot when my hands are cold?
Do temperature sensors get used to things?

faq.q: Why does mint feel cold and chilli feel hot?
faq.a: Menthol in mint switches on the same channel that cold sensors use, and capsaicin in chilli switches on a heat and pain channel. So they trick your sensors without changing the real temperature.

faq.q: Why does very hot or very cold feel painful?
faq.a: At extremes, pain sensors join the temperature sensors to warn that skin could be damaged. That is why ice held too long, or a hot drink, starts to hurt.

facts: Cold-sensing spots on the skin outnumber warm-sensing spots several times over.
Menthol activates a cold-sensing channel called TRPM8, and capsaicin from chillies activates a heat-sensing channel called TRPV1.
